title: Sorted Under a Custom Alphabet
statement:
A made-up language uses the 26 lowercase letters in a different order. order lists all 26 letters from first to last in that language.

Return true if words is in dictionary order for that alphabet. Two words compare at their first differing letter, by its place in order. If one word is a prefix of the other, the shorter word comes first. Equal neighbouring words are allowed.

examples.why: In this alphabet b comes before c, which comes before a.
"an" is a prefix of "ant", so it must come first.
The first letters already decide: b before c. The later z and a do not matter.

constraints: order is a permutation of the 26 lowercase letters
hints: A list is sorted exactly when every neighbouring pair is in order. You never need to compare words that are far apart.
To compare two words, you need to know quickly where a letter stands in the alphabet. Build a lookup from letter to its position.
For each neighbouring pair, find the first position where they differ and compare ranks there. If there is no difference, the first word must not be longer than the second.

explain.intuition:
Sortedness is a local property: if every word is at most its right neighbour, the whole list is in order, because the ordering is transitive. So the task reduces to comparing n − 1 neighbouring pairs.

Comparing two words under a custom alphabet is the same as the usual dictionary comparison with a different ranking of letters. Store each letter's position in a small table and compare at the first letter where the words differ. The one easy-to-miss case is the prefix: when one word runs out before any difference is found, the shorter word must come first, like "an" before "ant".
steps: For each neighbouring pair (x, y), scan positions until the letters differ.
At the first difference, if rank[x[k]] > rank[y[k]] return false; otherwise this pair is fine.
If no difference is found and x is longer than y, return false.
pitfalls: Comparing every letter instead of stopping at the first difference. In ["bz", "ca"] the later z and a would wrongly fail the check.
Missing the prefix rule and accepting ["ant", "an"].
Comparing with the normal alphabet out of habit. Every comparison must go through the rank table.

complexity.space: O(1), the rank table has 26 entries

solutions.title: Rank table and neighbour checks
solutions.idea: Turn order into a letter-to-rank table, then compare each word with the next at their first differing letter.

solutions.title: Translate to normal letters
solutions.idea: Rewrite each word so its letters become a, b, c… by rank. Ordinary string comparison then does the work, prefix rule included.

followups: You are given only a sorted word list, not the alphabet. How do you recover the letter order?
Sort the words under the custom alphabet instead of checking them.
